en: Now, by the phrase "familiarity consisting of injunctions and those to be enjoined," the commencement of an association in the form of mutual glances, conversation, and so forth, is proposed. Since that [association] will be rooted in the crushing of the tiger that has come upon Madayantikā, the entrance of Buddharakṣitā—who is connected to her—is intended to indicate Madayantikā’s readiness to go to the meeting place where Mādhava, Mālatī, and others are gathered. (1) [BUDDHARAKṢITĀ] "In the air. That which is a speech from afar, an incorporeal announcement, or a statement separated by something out of sight, is called "in the air" (*ākāśa*). (2)

Avalokitā: Do you know where the Blessed Lady is? Buddharakṣitā: Avalokitā, why are you so bewildered? There has been no time for the Blessed Lady to be anywhere other than following Mālatī, except during her mealtime. (The particle *ca* is used here for emphasis. *Bewildered* (*pramugdhā*): one who has forgotten. *Mealtime* (*piṇḍapāta*): the food obtained as alms by a follower of the Sugata.

Buddharakṣitā: Hum! And where have you set out for? (Hum—this is used for recollection. Avalokitā: Indeed, I have been sent by the Blessed Lady to the presence of Mādhava, and the Blessed Lady has instructed him thus: "Go to the garden named Kusumākara, which is connected to Śaṅkara’s house, and stay in the thicket of red aśoka trees at the edge of the kubjaka bower. And Mādhava has gone there.
Kubjaka: [B29b] A hunchbacked woman.

Buddharakṣitā: What about it? Avalokitā: Today is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; Mālatī will go to the temple of Śaṅkara together with the Blessed Lady. It is said that by doing so, one's good fortune increases. For the purpose of worshipping the deity, the Blessed Lady will lead Mālatī, accompanied by Lavaṅgikā, to that very Kusumākarodyāna garden under the pretext of gathering flowers with her own hands. But where are you going?
"Thus. By worshipping the deity with flowers gathered with her own hands.
Buddharakṣitā says: "And I was invited—meaning, summoned—by my dear friend Madayantikā, who had set out for the house of Śaṅkara."
Therefore, after I have paid my respects to the Blessed Lady, I shall go right there. Avalokitā: Regarding the matter for which you were appointed by the Blessed Lady, what is the news?

Buddharakṣitā: By the command of the Blessed Lady, during various confidential conversations, I was led to believe that her dear friend’s love for Makaranda is profound and remains hidden from his sight—love such as this and that. And her desire is simply this: "I wonder whether or not I might see him."
Avalokitā: Well done, Buddharakṣitā! Well done. Buddharakṣitā: Come, let us go.

[Kāmandakī]: So be it. Thus: in that manner, with decorum—that is, without any agitation or change of expression—and being humble, having attained a state of modesty, even Mālatī has been led by me, through various means such as the narration of the life-stories of Śakuntalā and Vāsavadattā and the description of Mādhava’s virtues, to a state of service—that is, to the abandonment of her modesty and reserve—by means of instilling a sense of confidence toward her friend, just as one would toward a companion. [1]

And likewise, he says "she goes" (*vrajati*) because those characteristics which Vātsyāyana described regarding a heroine who has displayed gestures and expressions toward a female messenger have now manifested. "Of us" (*naḥ*): in our separation. "Distraction" (*vaicityam*): a state of mental derangement. She sighs while brooding; she yawns; she becomes serene. Having seen [the messenger], she speaks with a smile. "In secret" (*rahasi*): she reveals herself in a secluded place. "Gift" (*dāyam*): substances such as camphor and the like. She complies.

The phrase "our mind" is the ellipsis to be supplied with "by practicing as described. Regarding the phrase "at the time of departure," it is because of the statement of Vātsyāyana: "He dismisses her with the expectation of a future meeting. (4) "Immediately" means swiftly. [2] [3] Regarding "Śakuntalā and others": having heard stories composed based on ancient accounts concerning Śakuntalā and others, her mind is distressed by the pain of love; due to her lack of physical strength, she remains for a long time motionless, holding her body close to my lap, wondering, "Shall I act like Śakuntalā and the others, or not? [3]
Uttarā: The next thing to be done.

Lavaṅgikā: Friend, look, look! This [wind] is indeed delightful, possessing the fragrance of Campaka flowers—slightly fierce yet tender—scattered by the encounter with swarms of restless bees that have flown up from the tops of mango trees, which are agitated by the clamor of cuckoos warbling sweetly and playfully as they devour clusters of fresh, moist blossoms.

The breeze from the Kusumākara garden embraces you—its movement faltering as its feet stumble under the weight of thighs heavy with the fullness of hips like those of a swan, its cool touch acting as sandalwood paste for the lovely moon-face of your countenance which is being anointed by drops of nectar-like perspiration brought forth by your smooth gait. Therefore, let us enter.

The syntactical connection is: "Indeed, this breeze from the Kusumākarodyāna garden embraces you. Regarding those [mango blossoms] which possess sweet nectar (*madhurasa*), the repetition of *ārdrārdrāṇām*—meaning "fresh" or "juicy"—illuminates their abundance. Of such *mañjarīs*, that is, clusters (*gucchānām*), there is the "taking in," that is, the consumption; in that regard, there is "play" (*keli*), that is, sport. By means of that, the *kokila* (cuckoo) has a "sweet" (*kala*) voice, meaning an indistinct yet melodious sound (*avyaktamadhurasvara*).

It was made charming by the fragrance of those *campaka* flowers, which had slightly assumed a formidable appearance—meaning they were on the verge of blooming—as their petals were partially split open due to the contact with swarms of restless bees. These bees, characterized by their habit of wandering here and there, had flown up from the tops of the mango trees, which themselves had been agitated by the great clamor arising from the abundance of sweet-sounding birds belonging to that [grove]. It was rendered enchanting by the scent of those [flowers].

By this, it is stated that due to the obstruction of the buds facing toward full bloom, their fragrance is faint. The reason why bees abandon the mango blossoms (*sahakāramañjarī*) to pursue the *campaka* flowers is that the former are crowded with flocks of cuckoos. Furthermore, regarding the swan: by the weight of bearing the broad and beautiful expanse of [her] hips, her two thighs—which are sluggish and languid (the implication being "your own")—have become unsteady and faltering in their movement.

By that—meaning by that smooth, very slow movement—there are brought forth droplets of perspiration; with these, your lovely moon-like face (*mugdhamukhacandra*)—the implication being "belonging to you"—is being built up as if out of drops of nectar. Therein, its touch acts like sandalwood due to its coolness; such is the meaning. (5) Regarding the term *binducityamāna*, it is derived from the causative form (*ṇyantāt*) of the root *ci* (to heap), meaning "those which are making it built up with drops," followed by the suffix *śānac*. Thus, because it manifests the coolness of the sweat-water clinging to the limbs, it is "cool.
[Mādhava: *Parāgatā*: she is present here, having arrived quickly.

[4] Previously, the sight of my beloved approaching brought contentment to my mind; now, as she approaches from behind, it is certain that she exists, serving as a cause for the joy of enthusiasm to behold her, since the entire burden of sorrow has been cast off—just as the flash of lightning, shimmering before a continuous downpour from the clouds, brings relief to the heart of a peacock distressed by the summer heat. (6) [4]

[5] In the proximity of this lotus-eyed woman’s face, my mind repeatedly attains a state of inertia characterized by an incapacity for all action; thus, a transformation—a change from its original nature—is brought about, pervading it. Just as, in the proximity of the stainless moon, a mountain undergoes a liquid transformation upon encountering the coldness of the moonstone—the *candrakānta* gem—so too does this occur here.

(7) By means of the simile with the mountain (*mahīdhara*), it is illuminated that the hero accepts the support of qualities such as fortitude (*dhīratva*) in the object of comparison. Here too, just like the behavior of the moonstone (*candrakānta*), when his own nature attains an entirely different state merely through the proximity of another object, that young lover experiences a sense of wonder.
[5] The word *saṃprati* is to be connected with "it sets ablaze" (*jvalayati*) and so forth.

[6] *Madayati*: it makes one joyful. *Parimalita-campaka-mālā-vilāsāni*: meaning they have become withered. *Lulitāni*: tossed here and there. Thus, it is a three-word *karmadhāraya* compound. (8) [6] MĀLATĪ: Friend, let us gather flowers in this thicket of *kubjaka* shrubs. [MĀDHAVA] [7] *Saṃśravaḥ*: hearing; by that, *sphurat-pulakaḥ*: with bristling hair (thrilled). *Ambaraḥ*: the expanse (of the sky). [7]
Lāvaṅgikā: We shall do so.

[Mādhava: But Mādhava—his purpose fulfilled by the mass of supreme bliss arising from gazing upon the thinness of Lavaṅgikā’s waist, the downy line between her breasts, and the base of her arms becoming visible as she raised them at the moment of gathering flowers—manifests his state of intense satisfaction, thinking, "The Blessed One’s mastery is of immeasurable wonder.
Mālatī: Let us gather flowers elsewhere than here.

[Kāmandakī]: In the meantime, Kāmandakī, wishing to dissuade Mālatī—who, having ascertained Mādhava’s presence there, desired to go elsewhere—under the pretext of mentioning her fatigue, says: "O, desist! *Nissahā*: one whose body is unable to endure fatigue.

[8] *Udbhāsanam* means adornment. *Vilasati* means it possesses the skill of manifesting its own activity. How so? It is "equal to the gaze of the beloved"; having made it like that, there is an intimation (*dhvani*) of the beloved's future gaze. For even that gaze is capable, as if it were a labor, of causing faltering of speech, looseness of every limb, perspiration, and the closing of the eyes like buds.
LAVAṄGIKĀ: The Blessed Lady speaks well.
The sense is: "Let it be desisted."
[Mādhava: Heart-touching: truly, because its form has been manifested, it is a delight to the mind.

[Kāmandakī: The chin: a part of the lower surface of the face. Regarding this, in the section on the duties to be performed by a female messenger (*dūtī*), Vātsyāyana has stated: "When her affection has been aroused, she should speak thus regarding the body of the matter: 'Listen, O fortunate lady; having seen such-and-such a person—the hero, the son of such-and-such a lineage—he is experiencing a madness of the heart. By nature delicate, he is a poor soul who has never before been tormented by another.'"

"Therefore, it can now be said that he is capable of experiencing death. Thus she speaks. (9) Then she proceeds accordingly. Mālatī: "I am attentive. [Kāmandakī]: "The Binding: the warding off of the mind intent upon the determination of the supreme reality."
Lāvaṅgikā: We remember.
[Kāmandakī] *Paravān*: one who is dependent, lacking independence.

[9] *Ānanda*: joy. *Priyaṅgu*: the *phalinī* creeper. Regarding *āpāṇḍutā* (paleness), he states its contrast with the paleness caused by disease; it is *madhura* (sweet) because it is pleasing to the heart. Furthermore, regarding *kṣāmatā* (emaciation), there is a contrast in that it is *ramaṇīya* (delightful). The repetition "emaciated, emaciated" (*kṣāmaṃ kṣāmam*) expresses a sense of progressive intensification. [9]
Lavaṅgikā: This too was uttered by Avalokitā at that moment, urging the Blessed Lady forward.

[Kāmandakī] [10] This: the moon-like face related to Mālatī; "certainly" means definitely; "has come to experience" means has been experienced, since—of this noble-souled Mādhava, whose heart is profoundly deep—the mind, through its yearnings (*ruharuhikābhiḥ*), is "trembling," meaning finding no pleasure anywhere else; it is "agitated," meaning moved from its natural state, just as [the mind of] a noble-souled one...
"The water of the deep and still great ocean becomes agitated, turbulent, and restless at the sight of the moon. (10) [10] [Mādhava:

"Purity" means freedom from affliction. "Greatness" refers to that which is comparable to the ocean, endowed with the quality of profundity. [11] "Firm standing" means the ability to perceive the limits [of a situation]. "Innate" means arising from prior practice. "Adaptation to time" means acting according to the opportunity. "Inspiration" (*pratibhāna*) means a timely flash of insight appropriate to the occasion. [11]

[Kāmandakī] [12] "He casts away" means he establishes. "Out of love for the forest fire" (*dāvapremṇā*): this refers to the notion that [the moonbeams] serve as a remedy against the forest fire. By this, the burning nature of the moonbeams is expressed. "Obstacle" (*antarāyam*): an impediment to death. For the moonbeams, by being the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) of passion, are the cause of misfortune. (11) Furthermore, because [the lover] is occupied elsewhere during the day, the onset of love (*kandarpāveśa*) in the mind does not occur to the same degree as it does in the night, which has become beautiful with the rising of the moon.

By this, it is indicated that the state of separation has reached its highest pitch, as it is established in a condition that transcends the initial stage, due to the agitation caused by life itself and because of the attachment resulting from witnessing the causes of death for the young mango tree and others.
[12] [Mādhava: "Unprecedented" means not previously experienced by others. "Mode of narration" refers to the context of the discourse. Mālatī: She performs a difficult task.
Because the sight of the young mango bud and so forth mentioned in the preceding verse has been experienced by Mālatī as well as being difficult to endure due to the unbearable pain of its burning.

By the phrase "never before afflicted by anything else," it is stated that this onset of passion toward you alone was his first undertaking. By the word "poor fellow" (*tapasvī*), it is stated: "This wretched man is a stranger; therefore, I say this out of compassion for him, and not from any other motive."

Mālatī: Friend, I have been terrified by the venerable lady, who, on my account, has announced some misfortune for him whose auspicious birth is the ornament of all the world. Therefore, what shall I do now in this matter?

[Regarding the word] *ātmanaḥ*: it means "of me. Although my mind is captivated by the sight of him and my life is dissolving through the affliction of being bitten by the poison of not attaining him, nevertheless, because of my maidenhood and the resulting lack of maturity, I am not capable of revealing my own condition. Thus, the sense is: "Dear friend, you yourself must speak."

Lavaṅgikā: It is reported that the Blessed Lady speaks thus. Our mistress, too, having frequently beheld him as he adorned the street near her residence for a moment, now—though her beauty is enhanced by limbs as lovely as the tender root of a lotus embraced by the rays of the sun, and though she is most alluring despite being afflicted by the pangs of love—distresses her attendants. She takes no delight in artistic pastimes; she passes her days merely with the circles of her cheeks resting upon the hands of her emaciated lover.

Moreover, she is distressed by the breeze from the edge of the palace garden, which is beautiful with the flowing nectar of blossoming lotuses and carries a multitude of droplets of honey from slightly opened *kunda* and *mākanda* flowers.

And on that day of the journey, there was a scene where the commencement of youth—rendered precious by its connection with a corresponding passion and delightful through various amorous sports—belonged to him who, having assumed a form for his own great festival, was like the Lord Kāma adorning the Kāma forest; a scene in which the curiosity of the hearts of those whose minds were distressed by the lack of opportunity to deceive one another’s glances descended upon them, while their limbs were slowed by the paralysis of rising trepidation, made beautiful by the clinging sweat, horripilation, and trembling, and which brought joy to the circle of her friends.

My dear friend has attained the joy of mutual gazing; yet from that moment on, experiencing a transformation of her condition that is especially difficult to bear, expanding, and intensely cruel, she withers away like a young lotus-plant at the rise of the moon occurring for but a brief moment.

Nevertheless, I know that the earth becomes cool as if being drenched by a torrential downpour of water—the intense joy arising from the commencement of a union with a beloved who has been conjured within her heart for but a moment—since [your face] is exceptionally beautified by the luster of rows of pearl-like teeth surging from quivering lips; since it is filled with a continuous stream of bliss-tears rolling over cheeks bristling with incessantly rising thrills; and since its blue-lotus eyes are slightly askance, motionless, languid, upturned, smooth, and closing like buds.

Bearing a charming lotus-face, beautiful with a new crescent-moon forehead adorned by lovely drops of perspiration breaking out incessantly, she causes doubt regarding her maidenhood to arise in the minds of her clever female companions. (13)

*Āliddham*: embraced; that is to say, touched. *Kandam*: the root; the meaning is "the lotus-fiber" (*bisam*). Indeed, the root of a charming young lotus plant is very slender, and it withers upon contact with the rays of the sun. By this—that which is embraced by the sun's rays—the root of the charming, youthful lotus plant is used as an illustration to express the lack of endurance and the slenderness of the limbs.

However, even in that state, there is a beauty that excludes other diseases; for that reason, the word *sundara* (“beautiful”) is used. “*Adhikaramaṇīyāpi*”: because the fact that the body is presided over by the bodiless god of love (*anaṅga*) is invariably accompanied by the full development of an excellence of luster. *Dūmedi*: it torments (*dunoti*). (14) *Kumilāyanta*: “withering away” (*klāmyat*); this is a regional term (*deśī*). In the reading *kamalāanta*, however, it means “becoming like a lotus” (*kamalāyamāna*), which is to say, “expanded. *Palhattham*: overturned (*paryasta*); that is to say, “thrown down. *Mākandam*: a mango tree (*cūta*).

The slowness of the breeze is described by its carrying a multitude of drops from the nectar of the *Aravinda* and *Kunda* blossoms, and by its connection with the edges of the palace garden, which provides both coolness and fragrance. "Having assumed a form" (*pratipannarūpaḥ*) means having taken on a physical body. Regarding the phrase "slightly contracted at every glance," Mālatī reveals the meaning just as Mādhava previously stated: namely, the mutual deception during the casting of glances. (15) "Jūravidam" means distressed; others read it as "jvaramāṇam" (feverish).

That which enters into such a state of mind is *kautūhala*: a restless longing (*ruharuhikā*). In the reading *tuvaranti*, it means "hastening"; the sense is that it arises quickly. =*Yathāyadi* = it withers. (16) *Nirmāyam*: free from illusion (*māyā*); the meaning is "true. It acted like that. (17) By the common expression *nirmāya*. For they say, having known it, "This is indeed the truth. Regarding *śītalāyate*: this too is by way of common parlance, as they say, for example, "A cool shiver has fallen upon my limbs."

(18) Displaying the signs of attaining sexual pleasure—such as the whirling of the circle of vision, the drooping of the limbs, the closing of the eyes, and fainting—he says, "jeṇa" (by which). The word *theva* is a regional (*deśī*) term used for both a drop and a small amount. (19) However, there is doubt regarding her state of maidenhood; for there arises the possibility that, according to the logic of Aniruddha, he truly becomes invisible and thus provides her with pleasure as a lover. Furthermore, there is an element of cleverness (*vaidagdhyam*), because this meaning—that these signs occur at the very moment the emotional state is perfected—is the exclusive domain of wit. (20)

Furthermore, she passes her nights in wakefulness upon a bed moistened with lotus petals and water, prepared by a company of female companions who hasten in their service—fanning her with young plantain leaves bristling with a spray of sandalwood juice, exceptionally cool and enriched with abundant camphor, while she wears a necklace of moonstones from which flows a continuous stream kissed by the mass of the unrestrained rays of the moon.

Somehow having obtained the pleasure of sleep, with the juice of *piṇḍālaktaka* oozing from her sprout-like feet due to perspiration, and with the knot of her lower garment loosened by the shifting of her thick thighs as they trembled, she—whose heart was being torn apart and whose long-lashed breasts heaved unevenly under the force of surging sighs—had cast her trembling vine-like arms around them in a binding embrace; yet, at the moment of sudden awakening, she cast anxious glances that perceived the bed to be empty, causing her eyes to close in a swoon born of despair.

When her fainting fit was interrupted by the efforts of her agitated friends, she remained with only her long-drawn sighs as the vestige of her life; thus, in her bewilderment as to what should be done, she first sought the end of her own life, making those like us merely occupied with censuring the irresistible and wicked play of fate.

*Kuṃbitam* means kissing (*cuṃbanam*). Or, because it has been kissed, its flow has begun. Sandalwood juice is already cool, but through the abundance of camphor, an even more intense coldness arises; thus, there is a state of excellence. By means of the plantain leaf—which is uneven due to the high and low surfaces created by contact with the sandalwood juice—acting as a fan (*tālavṛnta*), there is fanning (*saṃvāhanam*): that is, the setting in motion of the wind. In other words, it means fanning.

In that bed fashioned by her companions, who were hastening with their various activities, using lotus petals moistened with water—where *jalārdrā* means a wet cloth—the very state of sleep is "the bliss of sleep" (*nidrāsukha*), because it is the opposite of wakefulness, which consists of the suffering of agitation. Describing the signs of union with her beloved appearing in her dream, starting from her feet and extending to her eyes, he says: *seapajjhara*. *Pajjhara* means flowing forth.

(21) Thus, by virtue of being brought into the presence of her first leader, a tremor of awe arose in her such that the thick lac-dye on the soles of her feet was washed away by the breaking out of perspiration. The term *piṇḍālaktaka* is used to indicate its density. In some readings, the phrase is *tharaharāyantapīvarorupāsasiḍhilaṇīvibandhaṇā*; in that case, it means "the binding of the waist-knot became loosened at the sides of her thick thighs which were trembling."

Previously, perspiration arising from agitation was described; now, trembling is discussed. When there is trembling of the thighs or even the sides of the body, the loosening of the knot of the lower garment is a natural occurrence. "Ukkhalantaṃ" means being loosened or coming apart, because people commonly speak in that way when a painting or similar object separates from its wall.

(22) Thus, at the moment when the conditions for the interruption of sleep have converged, as the beloved begins to depart from her heart, she forms the resolve to restrain him as he prepares to flee. Consequently, by virtue of the surging sighs that momentarily ripple through her at that instant—unevenly, due to their manifold nature—as they both breathe upward, intent upon occupying the space of the sky above themselves, their eyes become thick with lashes.

The two breasts have their hair standing on end, and the *svastika* gesture of her arms is placed upon them. "Distressed" (*udvignā*) means not finding any pleasure anywhere. By the term "flowing together" (*saṃgalitatva*), he describes the simultaneous movement through both nostrils, because breathing proceeds in that very manner at the cessation of a faint. With the intention that she is known to be alive only through great effort, he says "attained with effort" (*prayatnapratipannā*). (23)

Behold, O Blessed One, how long will that Love (Manmatha) continue to have a favorable outcome, he who has displayed such cruelty toward these limbs of yours—so exceedingly delicate, fashioned from an abundance of loveliness? And how [long] these dawns, whose veils of darkness are shattered by the pure moonlight shimmering like petals upon the tender cheeks of Kerala women blossoming with the flush of anger during amorous play and quarrels? These...

"The nights of spring, which wash the courtyard of the sky with a brilliant moonlight as white as a mass of thick, flowing milk; which fill the ten directions with the Malaya breeze—made smooth and robust by its mingling with the intense fragrance arising from the crushing of fragrant *pāṭala* and *bakula* flowers; and which bring about the end of the spring nights—will prove to be the cause of my dear friend's misfortune."

*Paripelaveṣu*: in tender [parts], for it is impossible to produce an abundance of *lāvaṇya* (loveliness) in hard parts. *Kiyacciram*: after some time. Because the cheek (*kapola*) of a Kerala woman is naturally pale, its "sprouting" (*pallavitatvam*)—meaning it becomes as if covered in sprouts—is due to the redness produced by the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) of anger during a lover’s quarrel. By means of the Kerala woman’s cheek, which is naturally white but reddened by this adventitious condition, there is that which is "tender"—that is, similar—to it: the spotless moon, which is "shining," meaning rising.

By its moonlight. (24) *Parimalitam*: cultivated; that which is the crushing (*nirmathana*) or rubbing together of the *pāṭala* and *vakula* flowers; by that, there is the mingling (*miśrībhāva*) with the emission of a thick fragrance (*bahalaparimalodgāra*); by that, it is *masṛṇa*: moving slowly, and *māṃsalāyamāna*: assuming density.
(25) [Kāmandakī] [13] *Nanditam*: brought to joy; the connection is: "Even by this cruel state of hers, my heart is being torn asunder.
[13] [Mādhava] *Hṛllāsaḥ*: agitation of the heart.

[14] *Prakṛtilalitam*: naturally beautiful. That limb in which tenderness alone is the essence—that is, the stable constituent—is "tender. This is stated as a certainty (*satyam*), because he himself knows the deeds of Madana. (26) *Dāruṇaḥ*: merciless. One might perhaps endure the discharge of a single arrow; however, this one is unbearable, having in his hand many arrows known as "deluding," "intoxicating," "tormenting," "withering," and "slaying"—thus he is called the "Five-Arrowed One" (*Pañcabāṇa*). [14]

Lavaṅgikā: Furthermore, let it be known by the lady: this picture-board, which contains the likeness of Mādhava, and also this *vakula* garland worn around her neck—which was fashioned by his own hand—are both the very life-breath of my dear friend. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to join these two together. Regarding the word "fashioned" (*viracita*): for this reason [the garland is his].
[Mādhava: "With longing"—this indicates the intensity of her desire directed toward the state she has attained through the *vakula* garland.
[15] *Pariṇataḥ*: one who has reached full maturity. *Mugdhaḥ*: lovely. *Pariṇāhaḥ*: expansion; its *vilāsaḥ* is its unfolding; therein lies the banner (*patākā*). [15]

[Behind the scenes: O you people dwelling in the abode of Śaṃkara! Here indeed is he, having emerged from the monastery, his bodily form rendered terrifying by a fierce and formidable banner-like tail—thick, lofty, and quivering at its extremity through the playful sport of his own majesty; this tail which has shattered, burst open, and broken free the constraints of the iron cage and chains that had forcibly restrained the onset of an unbearable mixture of indignation and rage born of the dawning of youth.

At that moment, his cavernous mouth was made terrifying by fangs as hard as saws, amidst which lay the hard fragments of bones from the bodies and limbs of many beings greedily devoured; his throat-cavity was filled with the chewing of a forest of men, horses, and beasts mangled by his blows and swallowed whole like a fierce thunderclap, while the deep, gurgling, long, and sweet humming of the reverberating echoes from the interior of his throat terrified and drove away the entire multitude of people.

The wicked tiger, whose path of movement is mired in the blood released from the bodies of creatures mercilessly torn apart by the impact of his hard claws and shells, plays the role of Death himself. (27) Therefore, protect your lives to the best of your ability!

The connection is as follows: "This wicked tiger performs the sport of Death (Kṛtānta). By the force resulting from the mixture—that is, the blending—of those two unbearable qualities, intolerance and anger, which are produced at the onset of youth; by that force, the iron cage was shattered, meaning its bonds were loosened and opened. Through the breaking of the restraint of the chains, his own playful activity—a distinguished operation—was concentrated, meaning it was gathered together in one place.
